note: Lessons for the method modules. A lesson is exposition: it states the rules, shows how they fit, and hands off to the cards that keep them available and the problem questions that test whether they can be used. Every lesson carries its sources and a `verify` line — the app states a rule, it does not vouch for it.

lessons.title: How to study law, and why this site works the way it does
lessons.summary: Testing yourself beats reading again. A case brief is a discipline, not a summary. This site is built around both.

sections.keypoint: Law needs precise recall, structure, and writing under time — few subjects need all three.

body.text: Something has gone wrong — a deposit, a loan, a sacking, a piece of family land — so you read about it. Two weeks later almost none of it is left in your head.
Law asks three things of you at once. You have to recall it exactly, fit it to a situation nobody described to you, and then say it clearly, often in a hurry.

Very few subjects need all three, and a method that only builds recall will fail you here — slowly, in a way you will not notice. So this lesson is about the method: it is short, and it is worth more than any single rule below it.

body.prompt: You have two hours, and a chapter you read last week. Before you read on — which of these leaves more in your head a month later?
options: Reading the chapter again, slowly and carefully
Closing it and writing down what it said, then checking
Copying the main points out into clean, ordered notes
body.reveal: Closing the book wins, and it is not close. Re-reading feels far better, and that is exactly the problem. The second pass is smooth, and the mind reads that smoothness as knowing. If you picked it, you picked what almost everybody picks. The rest of this lesson is about why the pleasant option is the weak one.

body.title: Law asks three things of you at once
body.caption: Very few subjects need all three. A method that only builds recall will fail you here — slowly, and in a way you will not notice until it matters.
body.alt: Three demands, each depending on the one before it. Recall the rule exactly. Fit it to a situation nobody described to you. Then say it clearly, under time pressure.

steps.label: Fit it to new facts
steps.note: a situation nobody described to you

sections.keypoint: Trying to recall and failing beats re-reading, provided you then check the answer.
sections.h: Reading it again feels like work

body.text: The strongest finding in the research on learning is also the least obvious: reading a page twice feels like mastery, and leaves very little behind.
The feeling comes from ease. The second pass is smoother than the first, and your brain reads that smoothness as knowing.
Retrieval practice beats review. Trying to recall something, and failing, does more for retention than reading it again — provided you then check the answer.
body.source: Make It Stick; the retrieval practice literature

body.text: That is why this site hides the back of a card until you have answered. It is why a problem question makes you write the whole answer before the marking guide appears. Both are there to stop you reading the answer and mistaking recognising it for knowing it.
The uncomfortable part: study that feels harder is usually working better. If your revision feels smooth and pleasant, be suspicious of it.

sections.keypoint: Intervals grow because each successful recall makes the memory more durable.
sections.h: Spacing, and why the gaps grow

body.text: Say you meet a card on Monday and get it right. Meet it again on Tuesday and it is easy, so it teaches you nothing. Meet it on Friday, when it has half faded, and the effort of dragging it back is what fixes it.

Material reviewed at growing gaps lasts far longer than material crammed into one block. This site schedules cards on that principle, using a scheduler called FSRS. Each successful recall makes the memory sturdier, so the next gap is longer.
Space your reviews, and interleave topics rather than blocking them. Mixing contract and criminal in one session feels worse and produces better discrimination between them.
body.source: Make It Stick; the spacing and interleaving literature

body.text: Put simply: interleaving means mixing topics in one sitting. Blocking means doing one topic to death before moving on. Mix them.

Mixing matters especially in law, because the hard skill is telling one body of rules from another when the facts do not say which is which. A solid week of tort teaches you tort; tort mixed with contract teaches you to spot which one you are looking at.

sections.keypoint: A judgment read straight through like a news article wastes most of the time you spend on it.

body.text: A judgment is a court's written decision in a case. Reading one straight through, like a news article, wastes most of the time you spend on it.
A judgment has a structure, and you read it by pulling that structure out. Write these seven things down, in this order.

items: Facts — only the ones that mattered. A fact mattered if changing it might change the outcome. Lawyers call those the material facts.
Procedural history — which court this is, what it was hearing, and what the court below decided.
Issue — the legal question the court had to answer. Write it as a question.
Holding — the court's answer to that question.
Reasoning — why. This is the part worth your attention.
Ratio — short for ratio decidendi, the rule the decision rests on. State it so that it could settle a different case.
Obiter — short for obiter dictum, a remark the court made along the way. Note it, and mark it as such.

body.text: Puan Salmah's landlord keeps her RM900 deposit. She finds a judgment about a tenant who lost a deposit the same way. The year of that tenancy is background. The fact that the tenant left holes in the wall is material — change it and the case may come out the other way.

Write it down: a brief you did not write is a brief you do not have. Squeezing a judgment onto one page is where the understanding happens, and it also means you never have to read the full judgment again.
Do not brief from a headnote. A headnote is the summary editors print at the top of a law report; it is sometimes wrong, and it is never authority. Read the judgment.

body.q: You are briefing that case about the tenant who lost his deposit after leaving holes in the wall. Which fact is material?
options: The year the tenancy began
The holes in the wall
The court the case was heard in
body.why: A fact is material if changing it might change the result. Take the holes away and the case may well come out the other way, so they did the work. The year dates the case without deciding it. The trap is the third answer. Which court heard the case decides how much it is worth to you later. It is not one of the facts the decision turned on.

sections.keypoint: State the rule with its source, apply it to these facts, argue both sides, then answer the question asked.
sections.h: How to answer a set of facts

body.text: Sooner or later somebody hands you a situation and asks what the law makes of it — a friend, a form, a practice question. There is a shape that works.
Say what the legal question is, state the rule, apply that rule to these exact facts, and then answer. Those four steps are Issue, Rule, Application and Conclusion, which people shorten to IRAC.

Almost all the value sits in the Application. One common mistake is to state the law well and then stop; the other is to retell the facts without joining them to the rule. Application means saying which fact meets which part of the rule, and where it is a close call.
State the rule with its source. Apply it to these facts. Argue both sides where the point is genuinely arguable. Then answer the question that was asked.

Encik Rahim agrees on WhatsApp to sell his motorbike to a neighbour for RM2,000. He then sells it to somebody else. Issue: was there a binding contract? Rule: an agreement is normally binding where there is an offer, an acceptance and something given in exchange. Application: the messages show a clear offer and a clear yes, and RM2,000 is what was given in exchange. Conclusion: there was a contract, and Rahim has broken it.

That worked example is deliberately thin. A contract also needs parties who are legally able to agree, a genuine agreement free of pressure, and a lawful purpose. Those conditions are set out in the Contracts Act 1950, and a real answer would check them.

If you are studying for something formal, practise at the speed you will have to work at. An answer that needs ninety minutes is worth nothing in a forty-minute slot. Pace is a skill, and a clock is the only way to learn it.

sections.keypoint: Three layers: lessons state the rules, cards keep them to hand, problems test whether you can use them.
sections.h: What this site is and is not

body.text: There are three layers. Lessons state the rules and point you at the reading. Cards keep the rules to hand, and turn up just as they start to fade. Problem questions test whether you can use them.
The problems make you guess your own mark before you see the marking guide, and that is deliberate. When you learn on your own, your biggest blind spot is your view of your own work.
What this does not do is replace the books. The lessons are an orientation and say so; the depth is in the reading list.
Nothing here reads your writing, and no software marks your answer. The self-mark is honest only if you are, and the progress page says so rather than hiding it behind a number.

reading.where: the whole book — it is short and it is the evidence base for the method above
on reading cases, and on examination technique

lessons.verify: Nothing here is a rule of law and none of it needs a citator. The claims about learning are empirical rather than legal — if you want the primary studies rather than the summary, they are cited throughout Make It Stick.

Highlighting the key sentences

options: Be suspicious — smoothness is not memory

options: Mixing them teaches you to tell them apart
It covers more ground per hour

options: The judge repeated it
Changing it might change the outcome
Both sides agreed on it

options: It leaves out the facts
It is too short

quiz.why: Read the judgment. The headnote is an editor's convenience, not the court's words.

lessons.title: How a legal system is arranged
lessons.summary: Three splits that decide, before anything else, which rules apply and who has to prove what.

sections.keypoint: Before any rule applies, ask what kind of law the situation belongs to.
sections.h: Start by asking what kind of law this is

body.text: Two men argue outside a kedai runcit in Klang. One punches the other and breaks his nose. What happens next?
There is more than one answer, and both can be true at once. The police may charge the man who threw the punch, and the injured man may also sue him for the hospital bill and the wages he lost.
Those are two different cases, with a different person bringing each one, a different thing being asked for, and a different amount of proof needed.
So the first move is not to reach for a rule, but to work out which kind of law you are in. Three splits do most of that work, and none of them is hard.

sections.keypoint: Public law has the State as a party as the State; in private law the parties meet as equals.

body.text: The council refuses Puan Aminah a licence for her stall, which is her against the State. Her neighbour owes her RM800 and will not pay, which is her against another person.

The first kind is public law, which is you against the State: the Constitution, government decisions, crime. The second is private law, which is people against each other: contract, injuries, land, family, companies.
Public law: the State is a party in its capacity as the State. Private law: the parties meet as equals, and the State supplies only the court.
body.source: Standard classification; see Williams, Learning the Law

body.text: The line is not perfectly clean. A government department that fails to pay for the office chairs it ordered is sued in contract, like anyone else. The test is the capacity the State is acting in. A State body appearing on the page does not by itself make it public law.

sections.keypoint: Criminal proceedings punish and are brought by the State; civil ones compensate and are brought by a person.

body.text: This is the split most often blurred, because one event often feeds both. Keep them apart with two questions: who is bringing the case, and what are they asking the court for?
A criminal case is brought by the State — in Malaysia, by the Public Prosecutor, the office that controls all criminal prosecutions. It is brought against an accused, and it asks for punishment.

A civil case is brought by one person against another: the one who starts it is the plaintiff, and the one answering is the defendant. It asks for a remedy — money, called damages; a court order to stop doing something, called an injunction; or a ruling on where the parties stand, called a declaration.
Criminal: prosecution by the State, seeking punishment. Civil: claim by a private party, seeking a remedy.

A drunk driver hits a pedestrian in Ipoh. The Public Prosecutor charges him under the road traffic legislation. That is the criminal case, and the pedestrian is a witness in it, not a party. She separately sues him for her medical bills and lost income. That is the civil case, and the criminal one does not decide it.

Being cleared in the criminal case does not kill the civil claim. The two need different amounts of proof. Failing to prove something beyond reasonable doubt is not the same as showing it did not happen.

sections.keypoint: Beyond reasonable doubt for crime, balance of probabilities for civil — which is why one event can go both ways.
sections.h: How sure the court has to be

body.prompt: The same punch outside the kedai runcit is now before a criminal court and a civil court. Before you read on — how much proof does each one need?
options: The same in both, since both are deciding what happened
More in the criminal case than in the civil one
More in the civil case, because money is being taken off somebody
body.reveal: The criminal court asks for much more. If you chose the first, the instinct behind it is fair: it was one punch, and there is one truth about it. But a court is not asked what happened. It is asked how sure it must be before it acts.

body.text: Being charged and being sued do not demand the same certainty from a court. In a criminal case the prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt.
In a civil case the plaintiff has to show only that their version is more likely than not; fifty-one out of a hundred will do.
Criminal: beyond reasonable doubt. Civil: on the balance of probabilities — more likely than not.
body.source: Evidence Act 1950; standard common law formulation

body.text: The gap between the two is deliberate. A wrong conviction falls on one person and is close to impossible to undo. So the system accepts that some guilty people will walk free, in order to keep wrongful convictions rare.

The balance of probabilities really is a tipping point, and 51% is enough. Beyond reasonable doubt is not a percentage, however hard you press it. It describes a state of the court's mind, and judges have generally refused to put a number on it.

body.title: The two standards on one scale of confidence
body.caption: The same facts can fail a prosecution and win a suit. That is the system working as designed, not an inconsistency in it.
body.alt: A scale from no confidence to certainty, with the balance of probabilities just past halfway and beyond reasonable doubt near the far end.

sections.keypoint: Fact is what happened, law is what follows; appeals and precedent both turn on which is which.

body.text: The last split does the most work later and gets the least attention now. A question of fact is what happened. A question of law is what the rules make of it.
“The car was doing 90 km/h” is a question of fact. “Doing 90 km/h in heavy rain fell below the standard of a careful driver” is a question of law.
It matters for three reasons. First, appeals are often limited to questions of law, so how a point is labelled can decide whether it can be appealed at all.
Second, precedent — the rule that earlier decisions bind later ones — attaches to law and not to facts. A case is authority for its rule and never for its facts.

Third is history. Where trials had juries, this split shared out the work: the jury found the facts, and the judge ruled on the law. Malaysia has abolished jury trial, but it is why older judgments draw the line so sharply.
Fact: what happened. Law: what follows from it. Appeals, precedent and the division of labour in a trial all turn on which is which.

There is a third box: mixed fact and law. Asking whether 90 km/h was careless takes a fact and measures it against a legal standard. Where a point lands between the three boxes is fought over hard, precisely because so much rides on it.

body.q: A driver was doing 90 km/h in heavy rain. Which part of that is a question of law?
options: That the car was doing 90 km/h
That 90 km/h in heavy rain fell below the standard of a careful driver
Both, since the speed is measured against a legal limit
body.why: The speed is what happened, so it is fact. Whether it fell short of what a careful driver does is what the rules make of it, so it is law. The trap is the third answer. A fact does not become a question of law because a rule is later applied to it.

sections.keypoint: These three splits become the frame you read everything else in, so over-learn them now.

body.text: These three splits stop being a topic quite quickly and become the frame you read everything else in. That is why they are worth over-learning now, while there is time.
When you meet a situation, run them before you reach for any rule. Public or private? Civil or criminal? Which parts of the story are disputed facts, and which are disputed law?
Most wrong turns come from skipping that step. The five cards this lesson plants are deliberately small, and are meant to become automatic rather than thought about.

quiz.q: What makes something public law rather than private law?
options: Public law is statutory and private law is common law
Public law is criminal and private law is civil
In public law the State is a party in its capacity as the State

options: Prima facie; conclusive
Clear and convincing; preponderance
Certainty; likelihood
Beyond reasonable doubt; balance of probabilities

options: The parties are different
The time limits are different

options: It decides which court can hear the case
It decides the standard of proof

lessons.plateCaption: One building, two halves. Which side of the pediment a dispute falls on decides who sues, what must be proved, and to what standard.

lessons.title: What binds, and what merely persuades
lessons.summary: How an earlier decision binds a later court, which part of a judgment actually binds, and the four ways out of one.

sections.keypoint: A court is bound by the courts above it in the same hierarchy, on the same point of law.

body.text: Two neighbours in Seremban have the same argument about the same kind of boundary fence, five years apart. It would be strange if the courts gave them opposite answers.
So common law courts decide cases by looking at how earlier cases were decided. Like cases get treated alike. People can then arrange their lives knowing roughly where they stand.
The doctrine has a Latin name: it is called **stare decisis**, which means “to stand by things decided”.

body.prompt: Courts decide by looking at how earlier cases were decided. Before you read on — which earlier decisions must a Malaysian High Court judge follow?
options: Any decision of any court, here or in another common law country
Only decisions of courts above her in the Malaysian ladder
Only the decisions she thinks were rightly decided
body.reveal: Only what sits above her, on the same ladder. That leaves a great deal of law she may use and need not obey. If you picked the first, you were reading the daily practice correctly: English and Singaporean judgments are cited in Malaysian courts constantly, and often followed. Cited is not the same as binding, and the gap between those two words is most of this lesson.

body.text: Stare decisis: a court is bound by the decisions of courts above it in the same hierarchy, on the same point of law.

Three limits are packed into that sentence. Above it — precedent runs downwards, never up. In the same hierarchy — that means the same ladder of courts, so a court in another country sits on a different ladder. On the same point of law — a case decides what it decides and no more.
Almost every argument you will read about precedent is an argument about one of those three.

sections.keypoint: Only the ratio binds: the rule the court applied to the material facts to reach its result.
sections.h: Only part of a judgment binds

body.text: A judge decides Aminah's case and writes fourteen pages, but not all fourteen bind the next judge. Only the part the result actually turned on binds; the rest is commentary.
Test any passage by asking one question. Take that point away — would the case still have come out the same way? If it would, the point was not doing the work.
The ratio decidendi is the legal principle the court's decision actually rests on: the rule applied to the material facts in order to reach the result.
The word that matters is rests. The test is necessity, not length or force. A judge may spend four pages on a point that turns out not to matter, and settle the real issue in two sentences.

A ratio stated at the level of the facts is useless. “The council must pay for the blocked drain” binds no later case, because no later case has that drain in it. You have to state the rule broadly enough to cover a different set of facts. Choosing how broadly is where the argument usually is.

body.q: A judge spends four pages on one point, then settles the case in two sentences on a different point. Which is the ratio?
options: The four pages, since the court plainly thought them important
The two sentences the result actually turned on
Both, because both are in the judgment
body.why: The test is necessity, not length. Take the point away and ask whether the case still comes out the same way. The four pages could go and the result would stand, so they are commentary. The first answer is the trap, and it is a fair mistake to make. Length and force look like weight on the page, and they are not.

sections.keypoint: Obiter is anything the result did not require — quotable, persuasive, and binding on nobody.

body.text: Everything in a judgment that is not the ratio is a remark made along the way. It does not bind, though it can still carry great weight.
If the Federal Court comments on a point it did not have to decide, no High Court judge will brush that aside lightly. Lawyers call such a remark **obiter dictum**, “a thing said by the way”.
Obiter dictum: a statement in a judgment that was not necessary to the decision. Persuasive at most, never binding.

The clearest obiter is the kind a court flags itself. “We have heard no argument on this point and express no view upon it.” A court that says it is not deciding something has not decided it, however suggestive the rest of the page sounds.

The hard ones are the remarks nobody flags. A court that gives two separate reasons for its result has arguably given two rationes, and later courts will disagree about whether the second one was needed. Do not expect a clean line. Expect to argue about where it falls.

sections.keypoint: Binding means a superior court in the same hierarchy; everything else is persuasive at most.

body.text: Binding authority must be followed, whether the judge agrees with it or not. Persuasive authority may be followed. Its weight depends on which court said it, how good the reasoning is, and how close the facts are.
Binding: a decision of a superior court in the same hierarchy, on the same point. Persuasive: everything else — obiter, decisions of coordinate courts, decisions of foreign courts, textbooks.

Coordinate courts are courts on the same level as each other, so one High Court judge is not bound by another. In practice they normally follow each other unless convinced the earlier decision is wrong. That habit has a name, judicial comity, and it is good practice rather than an obligation.

Foreign judgments never bind a Malaysian court. This is worth saying flatly, because the daily practice can look otherwise. English, Singaporean, Indian and Australian cases are cited here constantly, and often followed. They are still persuasive only, because a different hierarchy cannot bind this one.

sections.keypoint: Four ways past an unwelcome decision — distinguish, overrule, reverse, per incuriam — and only one is usually yours.

body.text: You are before a judge, and there is an earlier decision squarely against you, and it is binding. What can the court legitimately do about it?
There are four moves and no more. Knowing them is the difference between arguing about precedent and reciting it.

items: **Distinguishing.** The earlier case turned on a fact that is missing here, so its rule does not reach this case. This is the everyday move, and the one you will use most.
**Overruling.** A higher court declares the earlier decision wrong. Only a court above the one that decided it can do this. Within limits, a final court can also do it to its own past decisions.

**Reversing.** An appeal court sets aside the decision below in the same case. This is not the same as overruling, and the two get mixed up constantly. Reversing happens inside one case. Overruling is about a different, earlier case.
**Per incuriam.** Latin for “through lack of care”. The earlier court decided without knowing of a statute or a binding case that would have changed the result.

body.text: Per incuriam: decided in ignorance of a statute or binding authority that would have altered the result. Such a decision does not bind.

Per incuriam is narrow. It is not a licence to ignore a decision you think is badly reasoned. The earlier court must have missed something it was obliged to consider. Bad reasoning is not enough. Overlooked authority is.

body.title: Four ways past a decision you would rather not follow
body.caption: Only the first is available to a court bound by the decision. The other three need either a different court or a defect in the earlier one.
body.alt: A question: a binding decision points the wrong way, so what is available? If the facts differ materially, distinguish it — any court may, and it is the usual move. If you are a higher court in a later case, overrule it, which only a court above the one that decided it may do. If it is the same case on appeal, reverse it, setting aside the decision below. If a statute or authority was missed, per incuriam — narrow, and not for poor reasoning.
body.question: A binding decision points the wrong way. What is available?

branches.label: Distinguish
branches.note: any court may; the usual move

branches.label: Overrule
branches.note: only a court above the one that decided it

branches.cond: a statute or authority was missed
branches.label: Per incuriam

body.text: This lesson plants seven cards, and they are worth being strict about, because precedent vocabulary used loosely shows very fast.

Then try the problem question. It gives you a short judgment and asks you to split the ratio from the obiter, and to say what a later court is bound by. It is harder than it looks. The passage most people mis-sort is the one that reads like an aside but was actually argued.

quiz.q: State the doctrine of stare decisis.
options: A court is bound by decisions of courts above it in the same hierarchy on the same point
A court must follow its own earlier decisions absolutely
All decisions of all courts bind all others
Precedent binds only where a statute is silent
quiz.why: Three limits: the same hierarchy, a court above, and the same point of law.

options: It is obiter
It was not argued
No later case has those facts, so it governs nothing
It is too general
quiz.why: A ratio has to be stated broadly enough to settle a different case.
quiz.source: Standard common law method on ratio decidendi

quiz.q: What is per incuriam?
options: Decided without reasons
Decided by a single judge
Decided on a concession
Decided in ignorance of a statute or binding authority that would have altered the result
quiz.why: It is narrow. It is not a licence to ignore a decision you think is badly reasoned.
quiz.source: Standard common law doctrine; the per incuriam exception

quiz.q: What is the difference between overruling and reversing?
options: They are the same thing
Overruling is by the Court of Appeal, reversing by the Federal Court
Overruling declares an earlier decision in another case wrong; reversing sets aside the decision below in the same case
Reversing applies only to criminal appeals
quiz.why: The two words get used interchangeably all the time, and the mix-up is always noticed.
quiz.source: Standard classification

quiz.q: Which of the four ways out will you use most often?
options: Distinguishing
Overruling
Reversing
Per incuriam
quiz.why: It is the only one open to a court that is bound by the earlier decision.
quiz.source: Standard common law method on precedent

lessons.plateCaption: The hierarchy drawn as steps. A court is bound by what is above it and not by what is beside it.

lessons.title: The words you cannot work around
lessons.summary: Five Latin phrases that each carry a whole body of law, and three kinds of story that should tell you at once which law is in play.

sections.keypoint: Legal Latin looks like a wall and is really compression: a whole doctrine in two words.

body.text: Legal Latin looks like a wall built to keep people out. It is not, though it is easy to see why it looks that way.
Each phrase below is a shortcut. One term names a whole rule, so that judges and lawyers can point at it without spelling it out every time. You cannot read a judgment at a normal speed without them.
Learn them as labels on drawers, not as translations. The point is not that you can turn audi alteram partem into English. It is that seeing it opens a whole drawer of administrative law at once.

sections.keypoint: Five maxims worth knowing cold — ultra vires, audi alteram partem, nemo judex, actus reus, mens rea.
sections.h: The five that earn their place

body.text: An Act gives a local council power to license food stalls. The council then uses that power to ban a stallholder from something the Act never mentioned. It had no such power. So the ban is not merely unfair — it is void, treated as though it had never been made.
Ultra vires — beyond the powers. An act done outside the authority conferred by the statute or instrument that grants it, and therefore invalid.

This is the engine of judicial review, which is a court examining how a public body's decision was made rather than whether it was right. A public body has only the powers Parliament gave it, and acting outside them is not just wrong; it is void.

Companies were historically caught by the same idea: a company could only do what its objects allowed. Modern company legislation has cut that back a long way. Treat ultra vires as fully alive in administrative law, and check the current Companies Act before running it against a company.
The next two go together. They are about how a decision is made, rather than about who had the power to make it.

A school expels a boy for something he says he did not do. Nobody asks him for his side of it. The teacher who complained also sits on the panel that decides. Two separate things have gone wrong there.
Audi alteram partem — hear the other side. Nobody should be condemned unheard.
Nemo judex in causa sua — no one a judge in his own cause. A decision-maker must not have an interest in the outcome.

Those two together are the rules of natural justice, which is the law's name for basic fairness in how a decision is made. Most challenges to a public body's decision are built on one of them. They are also among the very few rules you can rely on across common law countries without checking.
The last two split a crime into its two halves. Almost every offence needs both, and a prosecution that proves only one has proved nothing.

A man walks out of a shop in Johor Bahru with a phone he has not paid for. Taking it is one half of the question. Whether he meant to steal it, or genuinely thought it was his own, is the other half. Most offences need both halves.
Actus reus — the guilty act. The physical element of an offence: the conduct, and any required circumstances or consequences.
Mens rea — the guilty mind. The mental element: intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence, as the offence requires.

Those two together are what a prosecution has to prove. Take either one away and there is no offence. A man who takes an umbrella honestly believing it is his has done the act without the guilty mind, and he is not a thief.

Both criminal terms are less useful in Malaysia than a common law training suggests. The Penal Code defines each offence with its own mental element written into the section. The words still matter for reading the case law and for talking about how an offence is built. But do not go hunting for a general doctrine of mens rea in a code. Read the section.

body.caption: Learn them as labels on drawers, not as translations. Two of these go together as the rules of natural justice. Two more are the halves of an offence. The grouping is part of what the label is for.
rows: Beyond the powers — an act outside the authority the statute confers, and therefore invalid
Whether the body had the power at all
Hear the other side. Nobody should be condemned unheard
No one a judge in his own cause. The decision-maker must not have an interest in the outcome
The guilty act — the conduct, and any required circumstances or consequences
The guilty mind — intention, knowledge, recklessness or negligence, as the offence requires
The other half. Prove one only, and you have proved nothing

sections.keypoint: Issue-spotting is a memory problem: drill the fact cues until a situation names its own doctrine.
sections.h: Facts that should ring a bell

body.text: Spotting the issue is a memory problem, not a thinking problem. A real situation does not announce which body of law it belongs to. People rarely come unstuck because they cannot state the rules; they come unstuck because they never went looking for them.
So it is worth wiring a shape of facts to the law it should summon. Three to begin with.

items: A promise, something given in exchange, and someone who has not done what they said → contract. Ask whether an agreement was made, whether it can be enforced, and what the remedy is.
Someone hurt or out of pocket, and a question of who should have prevented it → tort, and negligence first. Ask about duty, breach, causation and remoteness, in that order.
A public body making a decision that hits someone, with something wrong in how it was made → administrative law, and judicial review. Ask about natural justice, and about acting within power.

body.text: Encik Lim pays RM500 to a man who promises to fix his roof. The man never comes. There was a promise and an exchange, so start in contract. Now change it: the man does come, works badly, and the ceiling later falls on Lim's daughter — so tort is in play as well.
These are starting points, not answers, and a rich set of facts will set off two or three at once. That is fine; the failure is setting off none.

sections.keypoint: Keep these cards short — if one takes more than a couple of seconds it is carrying too much.

body.text: The eight cards here are the shortest in the deck and should stay that way. If a card takes you more than a couple of seconds, it is carrying too much, so split it rather than keep failing it.
When one of these phrases turns up in your own writing without being reached for, it has done its job.

reading.where: the sections on legal language and on reading cases

lessons.source: Standard common law vocabulary; the Penal Code caution is specific to codified criminal law.
lessons.verify: Nothing here needs a citator. Before relying on the actus reus / mens rea framing in a Malaysian criminal answer, read the definition section of the offence in the Penal Code — the Code supplies the mental element expressly and the general doctrine can mislead.

quiz.q: Ultra vires means what?
options: Beyond the powers conferred, and therefore invalid
Against public policy
Without notice
Beyond the time limit for bringing a claim
quiz.why: An act outside the authority given by the statute or instrument that grants it.
quiz.source: Standard common law vocabulary; the ultra vires principle

That a decision-maker have no interest in the outcome
That reasons be given
That the decision be published
quiz.why: No one a judge in his own cause. Hearing the other side is the other rule, audi alteram partem.
quiz.source: Standard common law vocabulary; the rule against bias

options: The Penal Code defines each offence with its own mental element
They are Latin

quiz.why: You reason from the section, not from a general theory of the guilty mind.
quiz.source: Penal Code (Act 574); each offence carries its own mental element

lessons.title: The courts, and what each one can do
lessons.summary: The civil ladder from the Magistrates' Court to the Federal Court, the two High Courts, and the statutes that create them.

sections.keypoint: Precedent runs downwards, so the shape of the ladder has to come before the doctrine.

body.text: Precedent runs downwards through a ladder of courts. Until you know the shape of that ladder, the doctrine you learned in the foundations module cannot do anything.
Three things follow from this one diagram: which court can hear your matter at all, which decisions that court must obey, and where an appeal goes next.

body.title: The ordinary civil hierarchy
body.caption: Each court is bound by every court above it in the same line. The two High Courts sit level with each other: neither binds the other.
body.alt: The civil hierarchy, highest first. The Federal Court at the apex, where leave is usually required. The Court of Appeal, hearing appeals from the High Court. Then the two High Courts, side by side. The High Court in Malaya has unlimited original jurisdiction. The High Court in Sabah and Sarawak is coordinate with it, so neither binds the other. Below them the Sessions Court, which tries all offences except those punishable with death. Then the Magistrates' Court, for lower civil claims and remand under section 117.

rows.label: High Court in Sabah and Sarawak
Sessions Court
rows.note: all offences except those punishable with death

rows.label: Magistrates' Court
rows.note: lower civil claims; remand under s 117

sections.keypoint: Magistrates, Sessions, High Court, Court of Appeal, Federal Court — and the Federal Court is the apex.
sections.h: The civil courts, lowest to highest

body.text: Puan Siti is owed money by a customer who will not pay. She does not start at the top: a claim like hers starts near the bottom of the ladder, and only moves up if somebody appeals.

items: Magistrates' Court — the bottom of the ordinary ladder. Smaller civil claims and less serious criminal matters.
Sessions Court — above the Magistrates. A higher money limit, and a wider range of criminal cases.
High Court — no limit on what it can hear, and the first of the superior courts. There are two of them, dealt with below.
Court of Appeal — hears appeals from the High Court.
Federal Court — the top court of Malaysia.

body.text: Magistrates' Court → Sessions Court → High Court → Court of Appeal → Federal Court. The Federal Court is the apex.
body.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

body.text: There is also the Penghulu's Court, right at the bottom, with a tiny jurisdiction and almost no practical use today. Know that it exists, so a mention of it does not throw you. That is all it needs.

The money limits of the Magistrates' and Sessions Courts are figures set by statute, and they are raised from time to time. Do not memorise a number from a textbook. Look it up in the current Subordinate Courts Act 1948 each time you need it. A figure you learned three years ago is probably wrong.

sections.keypoint: There are two High Courts of equal standing, and neither binds the other.

body.text: Malaysia has two High Courts, not one. This is the fact that most surprises people arriving from an English textbook, and it is constitutional rather than administrative.

body.prompt: There are two High Courts: one for Malaya, one for Sabah and Sarawak. Before you read on — a High Court in Malaya decides a point. Must a High Court judge in Kuching follow it?
options: Yes, since both are High Courts and the ruling is High Court law
Yes, unless the Federal Court has said otherwise
No, because neither of the two binds the other
body.reveal: Neither binds the other. Precedent runs downwards, and these two sit level, so there is nothing for it to run down. A decision from Malaya is well worth reading in Kuching, and it is still not an order. The first answer is the natural guess if you think of the High Court as one court with two addresses. It is not one court, and the reason goes back to how the Federation was put together.

body.text: There are two High Courts of coordinate jurisdiction: the High Court in Malaya, and the High Court in Sabah and Sarawak.
body.source: Federal Constitution; Courts of Judicature Act 1964

body.text: Coordinate means level with each other, so neither binds the other. A decision of the High Court in Malaya is persuasive in Sabah and Sarawak and no more; it carries the weight one High Court judge's decision carries with another.
The arrangement reflects the terms on which the Borneo states entered the Federation, and it is a real feature of the system rather than a quirk of naming.

sections.keypoint: Courts of Judicature Act 1964 for the superior courts; Subordinate Courts Act 1948 for the rest.

body.text: The structure is not all in the Constitution. Two Acts do the work of setting out what each court can hear, and both are worth being able to name without hesitating.
Courts of Judicature Act 1964 — the superior courts: High Courts, Court of Appeal, Federal Court. Subordinate Courts Act 1948 — the Sessions and Magistrates' Courts.
body.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

body.text: The split is easy to hold once you notice what it tracks: one Act for the superior courts, one for the subordinate ones. That is the same line that decides whether a court's decisions can bind anybody at all.

body.caption: Which statute creates which court
body.note: The monetary limits of the two subordinate courts are statutory figures raised from time to time. Take them from a current source rather than from memory.
body.source: Courts of Judicature Act 1964; Subordinate Courts Act 1948

sections.keypoint: The Syariah courts are a separate ladder that does not feed into the Federal Court.

body.text: A second ladder runs alongside the civil one, with three tiers of its own.
Syariah Subordinate Court → Syariah High Court → Syariah Appeal Court.
body.source: State enactments; Ninth Schedule, List II

body.text: Two things about it are structural, and both get a lesson of their own later. First, these are State courts, created by State law, not federal ones. So there is no single national Syariah ladder, but a set of parallel State ones.
Second, they do not sit below the Federal Court, and no appeal runs from the Syariah Appeal Court into the civil courts. Two ladders, then, and not one tree with a branch.

body.q: Why is there no single national Syariah hierarchy?
options: The Syariah courts are created by State law, so each State has its own
Because Syariah law has not been written into statutes
Because the Federal Court has not yet set one up
body.why: They are State courts, made under State enactments, so the ladder is repeated State by State. That is also why no appeal runs from the Syariah Appeal Court into the civil courts. Two ladders, not one tree with a branch. The trap is the third answer, which treats this as a gap waiting to be filled. It is a division of subjects the Constitution makes on purpose.

sections.keypoint: Draw the ladder from memory once a week until it is dull.

body.text: Five cards, all of them the kind of structural fact that has to be instant. Draw the ladder from memory once a week until it is dull.
The reasoning that uses it comes in the next two lessons. Neither will make sense if you are still working out the order of the courts while you read.

options: Sessions → Magistrates → High Court → Federal Court → Court of Appeal

options: One, with two registries

lessons.title: Where Malaysian law comes from
lessons.summary: The Constitution on top, statute below it, English common law received up to a fixed date, and custom that counts as law.

sections.keypoint: Article 160(2) defines law here as written law, received common law, and custom with the force of law.

body.text: Pak Hamid's family has worked the same plot in Negeri Sembilan for four generations. They hold it under adat, the local custom, and there is no title deed in anyone's name.

Does that count for anything in a Malaysian court? You cannot answer from statutes and cases alone. The Constitution itself says what counts as law here, and the list is wider than a common law training expects.
Article 160(2): “law” includes written law, the common law in so far as it is in operation in the Federation or any part of it, and any custom or usage having the force of law.

Put simply, three things count as law here. Written law, meaning the Constitution, Acts and the rules made under them. The common law, so far as it actually operates here. And custom, where it carries the force of law.
The third is the one people forget. Custom is not a weaker thing that gives way to statute automatically: where it has the force of law, it is law.
The adat of Negeri Sembilan and the native customary law of Sabah and Sarawak are applied by the courts on that footing. So Pak Hamid's question is a real legal question, not a moral one.

sections.keypoint: The Constitution is supreme, and a later inconsistent law is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

body.text: Parliament passes an Act. Can a court throw it out?

body.prompt: Parliament passes an Act, and it clashes with the Constitution. Before you read on — what can a Malaysian court do about it?
options: Nothing, because Parliament is the highest lawmaker there is
Strike the Act down, so far as it clashes
Ask Parliament to think again, and apply the Act meanwhile
body.reveal: The court can strike it down, to the extent of the clash. If you picked the first, you picked the British answer, and it is the right answer there. No United Kingdom court can set aside an Act of its Parliament. Malaysia went the other way in 1957, and that single choice is what makes constitutional cases possible here at all.

body.text: In the United Kingdom, no: Parliament there is sovereign, and no court can strike down its Acts. In Malaysia the answer is yes, and this is the largest structural difference between the two systems.
Article 4(1): the Constitution is the supreme law of the Federation, and any law passed after Merdeka Day which is inconsistent with it is void to the extent of the inconsistency.

Merdeka Day is 31 August 1957, and an Act of Parliament can therefore be struck down. That single fact is what makes constitutional litigation possible at all, and it is the foundation of the fundamental liberties module later on.
Do not write that Parliament is sovereign in Malaysia. It is a common slip carried over from English texts, and it is wrong in a way that undermines everything built on top of it.

body.title: What outranks what
body.caption: Width here carries rank, not quantity. A law lower in the stack is void to the extent that it is inconsistent with one above it.
body.alt: Five layers, highest first. The Federal Constitution, supreme law of the Federation under Article 4(1). Acts of Parliament and State Enactments, within the lists in the Ninth Schedule. Subsidiary legislation, valid only within the powers its parent Act confers. Received common law and equity, under section 3(1) of the Civil Law Act 1956, to a date and so far as local circumstances permit. Custom having the force of law, under Article 160(2).

layers.label: Federal Constitution
layers.note: Art 4(1) — supreme law of the Federation

layers.label: Acts of Parliament and State Enactments
layers.note: within the lists in the Ninth Schedule

layers.label: Subsidiary legislation
layers.note: valid only within the powers the parent Act confers

layers.label: Received common law and equity
layers.note: Civil Law Act 1956 s 3(1), to a date, so far as local circumstances permit

layers.label: Custom having the force of law

sections.keypoint: Parliament and the State legislatures each legislate on their own list, with subsidiary legislation below both.

body.text: Below the Constitution sits written law. Parliament makes Acts, each State Legislative Assembly makes Enactments, and Sarawak makes Ordinances.
Who may legislate on what is fixed by the Ninth Schedule of the Constitution. It sorts subjects into a Federal List, a State List, and a Concurrent List that both may touch.
Parliament has two houses: the Dewan Rakyat, the elected lower house, and the Dewan Negara, the appointed and State-elected upper house.

Under the Acts sits a further layer. An Act may give a minister or an agency power to make the detailed rules: regulations, orders, by-laws. That layer is law, it is enforceable, and a great deal of the working detail lives there.
Subsidiary legislation: law made under authority delegated by an Act, by a minister or other body. Valid only within the powers the parent Act confers.

Suppose a local council by-law says a hawker in Penang must clear his stall by 11pm. No Act of Parliament says that. The by-law was made by the council under an Act that let it make by-laws. It still binds him.

Its validity depends on the parent Act. This is where ultra vires from the foundations module bites: acting beyond the powers you were given. Subsidiary legislation made beyond the delegated power is void, and challenging it is ordinary administrative law rather than constitutional litigation.

sections.keypoint: English common law applies only as it stood on stated dates, and only where no local statute governs.
sections.h: English common law, received up to a date

body.text: Malaysia is a common law country, but the common law did not drift in on its own. It was brought in by statute, and that statute fixes a date.

Civil Law Act 1956, s 3(1): the court shall apply the common law of England and the rules of equity as administered in England on 7 April 1956 for West Malaysia, 1 December 1951 for Sabah, and 12 December 1949 for Sarawak — so far only as the circumstances of the States and their inhabitants permit, and subject to such qualifications as local circumstances render necessary.

Put simply: English common law and equity apply here, but frozen as they stood on a date. That date is 7 April 1956 for West Malaysia, 1 December 1951 for Sabah, and 12 December 1949 for Sarawak. And they apply only so far as local conditions allow.
Two things follow. First, there are three cut-off dates, not one. Using the West Malaysian date for a Sarawak matter is an error anyone will spot at once.
Second, English decisions after the relevant cut-off were not received. They can be cited, and they often are, but they arrive as persuasive reasoning rather than as law that came in automatically.

Section 6 of the same Act keeps English land law out. Malaysia registers land under a Torrens system, in which registration itself creates the title. The English doctrines would cut straight across that.

Be honest about the complication rather than hiding it. Malaysian courts cite post-1956 English cases constantly. There is also a respectable argument that a later English decision merely declares what the common law always was, which would pull it back inside the cut-off. That argument is available to the other side. Meet it rather than pretending the date settles everything.

body.q: A Sarawak case turns on an English decision from 1953. Did section 3(1) of the Civil Law Act 1956 bring that decision in?
options: Yes, because 1953 comes before the 1956 cut-off
No, because the Sarawak date is 12 December 1949
No, because English decisions have never applied in Sarawak
body.why: There are three cut-off dates, not one. The first answer is the trap, and the one famous date invites it. The 1953 decision can still be cited in Sarawak, and a court may find it convincing. It simply did not arrive as law that came in on its own.

sections.keypoint: When a real question lands, work down the sources in order rather than starting with a case.

body.text: When a real question lands, work down the list in this order.

items: Is there a provision of the Constitution in play?
Is there a Malaysian Act on the point?
Is there subsidiary legislation made under that Act?
Is there binding Malaysian case law?
Only then: is there received English common law under s 3, and do local circumstances allow it?

body.text: Asked whether a landlord may do something, most people find a case first, because a case is what a search engine returns. The order above says find the Act first. A case cannot authorise what a statute forbids. Starting from the case makes it easy to miss an Act that nobody looked at, which answered the question outright.

sections.keypoint: Four cards, then two problem questions that lean on this material hard.

body.text: Four cards, then two problem questions that lean on this material hard.

One asks you to choose between sources when a custom, an old English case and a modern one all bear on the same matter. The other puts a Federal Court decision against a Privy Council decision and asks which binds. Both are more about knowing what a source is than about the law underneath.

options: Written law, the common law so far as in operation here, and custom having the force of law
Acts of Parliament only
Written law and subsidiary legislation
Statute and judicial decisions
quiz.why: That definition is the map of the sources, and custom is the limb people forget.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 160(2)

quiz.q: Which statement about Parliament in Malaysia is wrong?
options: Parliament has two houses
Parliament may legislate on Federal and Concurrent List matters
Parliament's legislation is subject to the Constitution
Parliament is sovereign
quiz.why: Supremacy belongs to the Constitution under Article 4(1). The slip is carried over from English texts.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 4(1)

quiz.q: What does s 3(1) of the Civil Law Act 1956 do?
options: Abolishes the common law in Malaysia
Applies all English law as it develops
Applies English common law and equity as they stood on stated cut-off dates
Applies English law only to commercial disputes
quiz.why: 7 April 1956 for West Malaysia, with different dates for Sabah and Sarawak, and only so far as local circumstances allow.
quiz.source: Civil Law Act 1956, s 3(1)

quiz.q: What is subsidiary legislation?
options: Law made by a State legislature
Law made by the courts
A draft Bill
Law made under authority delegated by an Act, valid only within the powers conferred
quiz.why: Its validity is always a question about what power the parent Act actually gave.
quiz.source: Interpretation Acts 1948 and 1967; the ultra vires principle for delegated legislation

quiz.q: What are the two houses of Parliament?
options: Dewan Rakyat and Dewan Negara
Dewan Rakyat and Dewan Undangan Negeri
Dewan Negara and Majlis Raja-Raja
Dewan Rakyat and the Cabinet
quiz.why: The elected lower house, and the appointed and State-elected upper house.
quiz.source: Federal Constitution Art 44

lessons.plateCaption: Four streams into one river: the Constitution, statute, the common law received to a date, and custom having the force of law.

lessons.title: Two court systems in one country
lessons.summary: Article 121(1A), what it actually says, and why it is not the blanket shut-out it is usually described as.

sections.keypoint: Two ladders of courts run side by side, and the Syariah one reaches only Muslims on listed matters.
sections.h: Two ladders of courts, side by side

body.text: A marriage breaks down in Perak. One spouse becomes a Muslim; the other does not. Which court decides what happens to the children?
Malaysia runs two sets of courts side by side. The civil courts you met in the last lesson are federal. They are set up under the Constitution and the Courts of Judicature Act 1964.
The Syariah courts are State courts. Each State creates its own by enactment. Their jurisdiction — the range of people and subjects a court is allowed to deal with — comes from the Ninth Schedule.

body.prompt: The Syariah courts are State courts, and their reach comes from the Ninth Schedule. Before you read on — who can be brought before one?
options: Anyone whose case raises a question about Islam
Only a person professing the religion of Islam
Anyone living in the State that set the court up
body.reveal: Only Muslims, and then only on the subjects the Ninth Schedule lists. Two limits, and both get dropped. The first answer is how the arrangement is usually described in conversation. That is worth knowing, because it is where most of the confusion here starts. A case does not change courts because religion turns up in it.

body.text: The Syariah courts have jurisdiction only over persons professing the religion of Islam, and only over the matters listed in the Ninth Schedule, List II, Item 1.
body.source: Federal Constitution, Ninth Schedule, List II, Item 1

body.text: Both halves of that sentence are limits, and both get forgotten. The power reaches Muslims, which is the limit by person, and it reaches only certain subjects, which is the limit by matter.
Those subjects are Islamic personal and family law, certain offences against the precepts of Islam, and matters tied to them. This is not a general power over anything with a religious flavour.

body.title: Two ladders, and where each one gets its power

items: Federal. Set up under the Constitution and federal law.
Their jurisdiction comes from federal law.
They reach everyone in the country.
General jurisdiction, across the whole range of subjects.
State courts. Each State creates its own by enactment.
Their jurisdiction comes from State law, never from Article 121(1A).
They reach only persons professing the religion of Islam.
Only the matters in the Ninth Schedule, List II, Item 1.

sections.keypoint: Article 121(1A) takes jurisdiction away from the civil courts; it grants the Syariah courts nothing.

body.text: In 1988 the Constitution was amended. A new clause, (1A), was added to Article 121. It is short, and it is quoted wrongly more often than almost any other provision.
Article 121(1A): the civil High Courts “shall have no jurisdiction in respect of any matter within the jurisdiction of the Syariah courts.”
Read it slowly, because it is a rule about overlap. It removes civil jurisdiction over matters that are inside Syariah jurisdiction, so it does nothing at all about matters that are not.
Syariah jurisdiction is limited by subject and by the religion of the parties. The reach of 121(1A) is limited in exactly the same way, because it borrows its boundary from theirs.

The common misstatement is “if Islam is involved, the civil court has no jurisdiction”. That is not what the clause says and not what it does. A dispute involving a Muslim party is not automatically within Syariah jurisdiction. And a non-Muslim cannot be brought before a Syariah court at all.

body.title: The clause is about overlap, not about Islam
body.caption: Both limits have to be satisfied before the clause does anything. The common misstatement is that the civil court has no jurisdiction whenever Islam is involved. That reads only the first half of the test, and often not even that.
body.alt: A question — is the matter within Syariah jurisdiction, by person and by subject? — branching two ways. Yes, a person professing Islam and a listed subject: the civil courts have no jurisdiction over it. No, either limit fails: Article 121(1A) does nothing, and the civil court keeps its power.
body.question: Within Syariah jurisdiction — by person AND by subject?

branches.label: 121(1A) does nothing
branches.note: the civil court keeps its power

sections.keypoint: Indira Gandhi: the clause does not oust judicial review, and cannot reach a person who is not Muslim.
sections.h: What the clause could not do

body.text: For roughly two decades after 1988, 121(1A) was read expansively. Civil courts declined jurisdiction in a run of cases where a party had nowhere else to go. Some of them were non-Muslims, who could not by definition appear before the court they were being sent to.
The Federal Court's 2018 decision in Indira Gandhi is the turning point, and it rests on something larger than the clause itself.

The power to review whether a public decision was lawfully made belongs to the civil courts by their nature. It forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution. A constitutional amendment did not remove it, and 121(1A) never claimed to.

Indira Gandhi: Art 121(1A) does not oust the civil courts' inherent power of judicial review; and the Syariah courts' jurisdiction cannot extend to a person who does not profess the religion of Islam.
body.source: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545 (FC)

body.text: The practical consequence is that a non-Muslim spouse or parent is not left with no court at all. The civil court decides whether an official act was lawful; it does not decide questions of Islamic law, and it is careful to say so.

body.q: A civil High Court is asked whether an official issued a conversion certificate lawfully. Does Article 121(1A) shut the court out?
options: Yes, because the certificate is a matter of Islamic law
No, because reviewing how a public decision was made is the civil courts' own work
Only where both parents are Muslims
body.why: Indira Gandhi holds that the clause did not take that power away. The court is not deciding a question of Islamic law. It is deciding whether an officer stayed inside the law. The trap is the first answer, which asks what the certificate is about rather than what the court has been asked to do.

sections.keypoint: Article 12(4) says 'parent or guardian', and the Eleventh Schedule is why that can mean both parents.

body.text: The fact pattern that keeps coming back looks like this. A couple marry under the Law Reform (Marriage and Divorce) Act 1976. One spouse converts to Islam, then converts the children, without telling the other.

Article 12(4): the religion of a person under the age of eighteen shall be decided by his parent or guardian — read with the Eleventh Schedule, under which the singular includes the plural, so the consent of both parents is required where both are living.

Put simply: a child's religion is decided by the parent. The Constitution writes that in the singular, but the Eleventh Schedule says the singular covers the plural. So while both parents are living, both have to agree.

That reading is what Indira Gandhi settled. It is a small piece of statutory interpretation doing a very large amount of work. It is also a good reason not to treat the interpretation module later on as an optional extra.

sections.keypoint: Two cards, then a problem putting a mother in the High Court against a 121(1A) objection.

body.text: Two cards, then the problem question, which puts a mother in the civil High Court facing an objection built on 121(1A).
The argument that wins is not about religion. It is about reading the clause as written, and noticing that the Syariah court's own jurisdiction has limits.

lessons.title: Finding the law, and knowing when you have not
lessons.summary: Statute first, case second, and the gap that makes free Malaysian sources unsafe to stop at.

sections.keypoint: Most bad answers begin with a search engine and a case that came back first.

body.text: You type a question into a search engine and a case comes back, and that is where most bad answers begin.
A case is evidence of what the law is, but the Act is the law. Research has an order, and almost every bad answer comes from working out of it.

items: Find the Act that governs the question. Read the section itself, not a summary of it.
Check the Act is current: the latest reprint, any amending Acts, and whether an amendment has actually come into force.
Look for subsidiary legislation made under it. The working detail often lives there.
Then find the cases. Place each one: which court, what year, ratio or remark made by the way.
Then check whether those cases are still good law.

body.text: Someone asks whether a landlord may seize goods for unpaid rent without going to court. A search turns up a High Court decision that appears to say yes. The governing instrument is the Distress Act 1951, and it routes the landlord through an application to the court. Starting from the case made it possible to miss the Act entirely.

sections.keypoint: Use the Attorney General's Chambers portal for statute — it is the official text and it is free.
sections.h: Where to get the text, free

body.text: You do not need a paid subscription to read a Malaysian Act, because the Government publishes them free.
The official text of Malaysian Acts is published free by the Attorney General's Chambers on its portal. That is the source to use for statute.
Free sources for cases exist too, and they are genuinely useful for reading a judgment. What they are not is complete, and the gap is a specific one that is worth knowing exactly.

body.prompt: You find a 2003 High Court judgment on a free portal. It answers your question exactly, and nothing on the page warns you about it. Before you read on — what does that silence tell you?
options: That the case is still good law, or the portal would say so
Nothing at all about whether the case still stands
That nobody appealed it
body.reveal: It tells you nothing. The portal shows you the judgment. It does not track what later courts did with it. If you picked the first, that is how these pages get used every working day. It is the most expensive assumption in free research. No warning is not a clean bill of health. It is the absence of anybody looking.

sections.keypoint: Noting up means checking what later courts did with a case, and it is the step people skip.
sections.h: Nothing free tells you the case still stands

body.text: You find a 2003 High Court decision that answers your question perfectly. What the page cannot tell you is that the Court of Appeal reversed it two years later.

There is a tool for this. A citator tells you what happened to a case afterwards: appealed, reversed, overruled, distinguished, followed, or merely doubted — and running a case through one is called noting up.
Noting up: checking a case's subsequent judicial treatment to establish whether it is still good law.
You cannot confirm from free Malaysian sources alone that a case is still good law. There is no free citator. That check requires CLJ, LexisNexis CaseBase, or Westlaw Asia.
body.source: Practice; the constraint is commercial, not legal

body.text: The dangerous inference is the silent one. A free portal showing no overruling is not evidence that there was none; it is evidence that the portal does not track overruling. Absence of a warning is not a clean bill of health.

None of this is a reason to avoid free sources. It is a reason to know exactly what they cannot tell you, and to say so when you report. An answer that states its own limits is worth more than one that quietly has them.

body.title: What free sources can and cannot tell you

items: The official text of Malaysian Acts, published free by the Attorney General's Chambers.
Judgments you can read in full.
Enough to find the provision and place the cases.
Genuinely useful, and the right place to start.
Whether a case was later reversed, overruled or doubted.
There is no free Malaysian citator.
**Silence is not evidence.** A portal showing no overruling is not evidence there was none.
That check needs CLJ, LexisNexis CaseBase, or the equivalent.

sections.keypoint: When there is no time for a full check, say what you checked and what you did not.
sections.h: Answering when the time has run out

body.text: You will often be asked something with less time than a full check needs. Refusing to answer is not the right response, and neither is answering as though the check had been done.

The form that works has four parts. Here is the provision that governs it, and what it says. Here is the case law I found, and where each case sits in the hierarchy. Here is what I could not verify, and the tool that would be needed. And here is what I would not advise on this basis.
That is a bounded answer, and it is also what the problem question in this module asks you to produce.

body.title: The four parts of a bounded answer

items.text: Name the section that governs the question, and say what it provides. The Act is the law; a case is evidence of what it means.
Place each case: which court, what year, and whether the point was the ratio or a remark made by the way.
Say which check is missing and name the tool it would need. For subsequent treatment that means a citator, and there is no free one.

items.h: What you would not advise on this basis.
items.text: State the limit rather than leaving it implied. An answer with its boundary drawn is useful; one that hides the boundary is not.

sections.keypoint: Three cards about where to look and what the limits are, rather than about any rule.

body.text: Three cards, which are about where to look and what the limits are, rather than about any rule of law.
Then the problem question, whose answer is a method rather than a proposition. It is the only one in the set where reaching the right conclusion earns almost nothing if the order of work was wrong.
